title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
summary:
OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today. 
 One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety . Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week.
 The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment , rather than how many restrictions you impose.

title: Tree Appreciator
summary:
Tool: Tree Appreciator 

 Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with:

 Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. 

 Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play.

title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
summary:
A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack , and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding , or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is . Their substack — or at least Owl Posting ’s 1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI.
 
 So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules. 2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing.
 It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
summary:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. 

Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).

 I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

 Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]

 This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[

 With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.

 Via Hacker News 

 Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
summary: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions.
